title: The Calibration Problem in Radiocarbon Dating
paragraphs: A few milligrams of charred wheat from a storeroom that burned three thousand years ago can name the century of the fire.
The mechanism is almost too tidy.
Living things take in carbon.
A tiny, constant fraction of that carbon is unstable.
When the organism dies the intake stops and that fraction thins out on a fixed schedule.
Measure what is left, work backward, and the grain gives up its date.
The word carrying the trouble in that summary is constant.
Carbon fourteen is manufactured continuously overhead.
Cosmic rays smash into nuclei in the upper atmosphere and knock loose free neutrons.
A neutron that strikes a nitrogen fourteen nucleus can lodge there and expel a proton, leaving a nucleus of the same total mass but one fewer unit of positive charge: carbon fourteen.
It is soon oxidized to carbon dioxide, and within a few years mixing carries it worldwide.
A plant takes in carbon fourteen in close to the proportion the air offers, animals acquire it by eating plants, and every living body tops up its supply as long as it feeds.
The result is an internal ratio near the atmosphere's own, roughly one carbon fourteen atom per trillion of ordinary carbon twelve.
Death closes the account.
Nothing new comes in, and the carbon fourteen already present decays on its own timetable, an electron flying off as each atom turns back into nitrogen fourteen.
Half of any population of these atoms is gone in about 5,730 years.
There is a wrinkle, though.

The earliest measurements put the half-life near 5,568 years, and though the better figure has long been known, laboratories still report ages calculated from the original value, so dates published half a century apart stay comparable.
After ten halvings only about a thousandth of the original carbon fourteen survives, which sets a practical ceiling near fifty thousand years.
The method is also particular about its subject, dating only carbon that once exchanged with the atmosphere: charcoal, wood, seed, bone, shell, cloth and parchment.

All of this rests on knowing how much carbon fourteen the air held when the organism died, and the founding assumption was the simplest one available: that production and decay had long since balanced, leaving the atmospheric level fixed.
That is a sensible first approximation, and it is wrong.
Production depends on how many cosmic rays get through.
The earth's magnetic field deflects them, and its strength has drifted over the last ten thousand years.
The sun's outflowing wind deflects them as well, so an active sun suppresses production and a quiet sun raises it.
Egyptian objects whose calendar dates were already fixed by written records came back from the laboratory too young, some by several centuries.
The conclusion was unavoidable: a radiocarbon year is not a calendar year, and the gap between them is not a constant.
The correction came from trees.
A temperate tree lays down one ring a year, wide in a good season and narrow in a bad one, so a run of rings records fat and lean years.
Every tree alive through those seasons shares the pattern, so a living tree can be matched to an old beam, the beam to a buried log, and so on backward.
Stitched together, European oak and pine carry an unbroken year by year record back more than twelve thousand years.
Measuring carbon fourteen in rings of known age turns the problem into a graph, and it is not the straight line the founding assumption predicted.
It wobbles.

Decades of weak solar activity leave bumps in it, and in places the curve flattens into a plateau, a stretch where the atmospheric level barely changed, so that many different calendar years produce nearly the same radiocarbon result.
One notorious flat stretch covers roughly four centuries, from about 800 to 400 before the common era.
A sample from anywhere inside it returns almost the same answer, and the calendar range that comes back is four centuries wide however careful the laboratory was.
Trees run out before the method does.
For older material the curve is carried forward by other archives, among them corals dated independently by uranium and thorium.
The agreed curve now runs to about fifty five thousand years.
Some carbon came from the air long ago or never at all, and organisms feeding on such a reservoir inherit its head start.
Deep ocean water has been out of contact with the atmosphere for centuries, so carbon from the sea is already old when a clam builds a shell from it.
Marine organisms therefore appear roughly four hundred years dead at the moment they actually die.

Fresh water can be worse: a lake fed by springs running through limestone carries dissolved carbonate with no carbon fourteen in it at all, and shells from such a lake have come back thousands of years too old.
Human activity has since moved the level far more violently than the sun ever did.
Nuclear weapons tested in the open air released floods of neutrons, making carbon fourteen exactly as cosmic ray neutrons do.
By 1963 the northern hemisphere's atmospheric level had nearly doubled.
A treaty signed that year drove testing underground, and the excess has since drained away until the air is close to its level before the tests.
That steep decline is a gift.

Each year on the descending limb carries its own value, so tissue grown in the last seventy years can often be placed within a year or two, which is how tooth enamel, laid down in childhood and never rebuilt, has been used to estimate a person's year of birth.
A second human signal runs the opposite way.

Coal, oil and gas formed so long ago that every carbon fourteen atom in them decayed away ages back, which makes their carbon dead in the only sense that matters here: it carries no radiocarbon whatever.
Burning them pours dead carbon into the air and dilutes the living fraction, so the atmosphere takes on an apparent age it did not earn.

With the bomb carbon nearly gone, dilution is now the dominant trend, and if emissions continue, cloth made later this century could carry the radiocarbon signature of something several hundred years old.
The laboratory must also defend the sample, and the threats are lopsided.
Recent carbon is the dangerous intruder.
One percent of modern carbon mixed into a sample that is truly forty thousand years old brings back a reported age near thirty two thousand, an error of eight millennia.
One percent of dead carbon mixed into a modern sample shifts its reported age by about eighty years.
Rootlets, groundwater humic acids and old glues all deliver carbon of the wrong age, so pretreatment is no formality: acid and alkali washes strip the soluble intruders.

Sample choice matters just as much: the heartwood of a beam grew centuries before the tree was felled, and beams were often salvaged and reused, so a seed, which lives one season, answers a sharper question.
The instrument changed as well.
Counting decays meant grams of purified carbon and days of waiting.
Accelerator mass spectrometry counts the atoms themselves, so a milligram is enough.
What the laboratory hands back, then, is not a year.
It is a measurement, reported in a form such as 2450 plus or minus 30 before present, with present fixed by convention at 1950.
The plus or minus describes the precision of the counting, and it is tempting to read it as the calendar answer's error bar.
It is not.
That symmetrical bell has to be pushed through the wobbling calibration curve first, and what emerges is lumpy: sometimes one narrow interval, sometimes two or three humps with gaps between them.
The intuition that a better measurement always buys a better date fails outright on a plateau, where halving the counting error barely narrows the calendar range.
An honest radiocarbon date is therefore a probability distribution, normally quoted as the intervals holding sixty eight and ninety five percent of it.
And the atmosphere's refusal to hold still, the flaw that made all of this necessary, turned out to be worth having.
The calibration curve is itself a record of the sun, the magnetic field and the ocean.
The correction and the archive are the same object.

questions.stem: According to the passage, carbon fourteen forms in the upper atmosphere when
choices: nitrogen fourteen absorbs a passing electron and grows heavier by one unit of mass
a cosmic ray proton is captured directly by a carbon twelve nucleus
high energy radiation splits carbon dioxide molecules apart in the stratosphere
a free neutron enters a nitrogen fourteen nucleus and drives out a proton
particles in the solar wind attach a neutron to a nucleus of carbon thirteen

proof.quote: A neutron that strikes a nitrogen fourteen nucleus can lodge there and expel a proton

questions.why: Paragraph 2 walks the step through in order: cosmic rays knock free neutrons loose, and a neutron that strikes a nitrogen fourteen nucleus lodges there and expels a proton. Same total mass, one fewer unit of positive charge, which makes it carbon.
distractorNotes: This runs the paragraph 4 decay step backward, and no electron is absorbed anywhere in the passage.
Cosmic rays start the chain, but the passage has them shattering nuclei to release neutrons rather than being captured by carbon.
Carbon dioxide is where the new atom ends up after it forms, not the raw material it is made from.
Paragraph 6 gives the solar wind the opposite role, deflecting cosmic rays and lowering production rather than building the isotope.

questions.stem: The passage says laboratories still calculate reported ages from a half-life near 5,568 years because
choices: modern measurements have confirmed that this is the accurate figure
the shorter value offsets the effect of contamination by recent carbon
holding to the original value keeps dates published decades apart comparable
the calibration curve is built on the assumption that the atmosphere never changed
decay counting instruments cannot resolve the difference between the two figures

proof.quote: so dates published half a century apart stay comparable
though the better figure has long been known

questions.why: Paragraph 4 calls it a wrinkle and gives the reason outright: the original value is kept so that dates published half a century apart stay directly comparable, even though about 5,730 years is the better figure.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 4 names 5,730 years as the better figure, so the value actually used is the one known to be slightly off.
Contamination is a paragraph 14 problem, handled by pretreatment, not by the choice of a half-life.
Calibration exists precisely because the atmosphere did change, as paragraphs 6 and 9 both insist.
The passage never blames the instruments for this choice, since paragraph 4 gives comparability as the whole reason.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a sample that is truly forty thousand years old but carries one percent modern carbon comes back with a reported age of about
choices: eight thousand years
thirty nine thousand years
forty eight thousand years
thirty two thousand years
forty thousand years, since a one percent intruder is too small to matter

proof.quote: brings back a reported age near thirty two thousand

questions.why: Paragraph 14 supplies that number to show how lopsided the threat is. One percent of modern carbon drags a forty thousand year old sample down to roughly thirty two thousand, an error of eight millennia.
distractorNotes: Eight thousand is the size of the error, not the age that comes back.
A thousand year error would be the mild outcome, and the passage puts the shift at eight thousand years.
Modern carbon adds carbon fourteen, so it always makes a sample look younger rather than older.
This is the intuition paragraph 14 is written to overturn, since a tiny intruder produces an enormous shift.

questions.stem: The passage attributes the fact that shells from a limestone fed lake can come back thousands of years too old to
choices: the unusual pressure under which lake shells build their carbonate
the slow turnover of the deep ocean water that feeds the lake
dissolved carbonate in the spring water with no carbon fourteen
a locally high rate of carbon fourteen production over inland regions
contamination of the shells by rootlets and by groundwater

proof.quote: dissolved carbonate with no carbon fourteen in it at all

questions.why: Paragraph 11 treats it as a reservoir effect. Springs running through limestone carry dissolved carbonate with no carbon fourteen in it at all, so shells built from that carbon start out looking ancient.
distractorNotes: Pressure plays no part in anything the passage describes.
Deep ocean water is the marine case in the same paragraph, and a spring fed lake is a separate reservoir.
Paragraph 2 says mixing carries the isotope worldwide within a few years, so no region has its own elevated supply.
Rootlets and groundwater are paragraph 14 contaminants, and those tend to add recent carbon, which makes a sample look younger.

questions.stem: According to the passage, by 1963 the northern hemisphere's atmospheric carbon fourteen level had
choices: returned to where it stood before the weapons tests began
roughly doubled
fallen by about half
stopped changing in any measurable way
risen by the equivalent of four hundred years of decay

proof.quote: had nearly doubled

questions.why: Paragraph 12 gives the figure plainly: neutrons from open air weapons testing had nearly doubled the northern hemisphere's atmospheric level by 1963.
distractorNotes: The return toward the pre-test level came afterward, once the treaty drove testing underground.
Nothing halved, since the tests added carbon fourteen to the air rather than removing it.
The level was moving faster than at any other point in the passage, which is what makes the descending limb useful.
Four hundred years is the marine offset from paragraph 11, a different quantity in a different context.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 9, "plateau" most nearly means
choices: a flat stretch where many calendar years share one radiocarbon value
a gap in the tree ring record that no surviving piece of timber can bridge
a broad raised area of level ground in a landscape
the highest value that the curve ever reaches
the age past which the method stops working entirely

proof.quote: many different calendar years produce nearly the same radiocarbon result

questions.why: Paragraph 9 defines the word where it uses it: a stretch of curve where the atmospheric level barely changed, so many different calendar years produce nearly the same radiocarbon result.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 8 describes the tree ring record as unbroken, so no such gap is at issue.
This is the everyday landform sense the passage is borrowing from, not the sense it puts to work.
A flat stretch is level, not high, and nothing in paragraph 9 makes it a maximum.
A sample inside a plateau still returns an answer; the answer is just spread across four centuries.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 13, carbon called "dead" is carbon that
choices: comes from organisms that stopped feeding only recently
can no longer take part in any chemical reaction
has been stripped out of a sample during pretreatment
sits sealed away from the air while it goes on decaying
contains no detectable carbon fourteen

proof.quote: it carries no radiocarbon whatever

questions.why: Paragraph 13 states the sense it intends in the same sentence: coal, oil and gas are so old that every carbon fourteen atom in them decayed away long ago, so their carbon carries no radiocarbon whatever.
distractorNotes: Recently dead material is the opposite case, since its carbon is still rich in carbon fourteen.
Fossil carbon burns readily, which is the whole problem, so chemical inertness is not the point.
Pretreatment in paragraph 14 removes intruders; it does not create the carbon the passage calls dead.
The point is that the decay finished ages ago, not that it is still running out of sight.

questions.stem: The passage's account of contamination most strongly supports which statement about an ancient sample that takes up a trace of recent carbon
choices: no pretreatment can remove an intruder of this kind
the sample will come back much younger than it really is
the error will match what an equal trace of ancient carbon would cause
the sample will come back older than it really is
the error will stay small because the intruding amount is small

proof.quote: Recent carbon is the dangerous intruder.
an error of eight millennia
shifts its reported age by about eighty years

questions.why: Paragraph 14 runs the arithmetic in one direction only. Recent carbon adds carbon fourteen that the old sample should not have, so the reported age is pulled toward the present, by eight thousand years in the example given.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 14 describes acid and alkali washes stripping the soluble intruders, so such samples are not written off.
The passage calls the threats lopsided and gives the two figures, eight thousand years against about eighty.
Adding carbon fourteen makes a sample look younger; only dead carbon can push an age older.
Paragraph 14 chooses the one percent example precisely because a tiny intruder produces an enormous shift.

questions.stem: Based on paragraph 9, two pieces of charcoal burned three hundred years apart, both inside that flat stretch, would most likely
choices: come back three hundred years apart, matching their true separation
prove impossible for a laboratory to measure at all
differ by far more than the laboratory's stated uncertainty
land on two separate humps of one calibrated distribution
come back with radiocarbon results too close to tell apart

proof.quote: A sample from anywhere inside it returns almost the same answer

questions.why: Paragraph 9 says a sample from anywhere inside the flat stretch returns almost the same answer, which is why the calendar range stays four centuries wide. Two samples three hundred years apart in there would be very hard to tell apart.
distractorNotes: That is what a straight calibration line would deliver, and paragraph 9 says the curve is flat across this span instead.
The measurement itself is fine; it is the translation onto a calendar that stays wide.
A plateau compresses real differences rather than exaggerating them.
Separate humps belong to paragraph 16, where a wiggle splits a distribution, not to a flat stretch.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the central point of the passage
choices: Tree rings are the most valuable archive available anywhere in the earth sciences
The chemistry behind carbon fourteen production is more intricate than most people realize
Nuclear weapons testing did permanent damage to the usefulness of radiocarbon dating
Radiocarbon dating has been compromised by human pollution to the point where recent material can no longer be trusted
A radiocarbon date is a corrected range rather than a year, because the method's founding assumption is false

proof.quote: The word carrying the trouble in that summary is constant.
That is a sensible first approximation, and it is wrong.
What the laboratory hands back, then, is not a year.
An honest radiocarbon date is therefore a probability distribution

questions.why: The passage moves in one direction throughout: a tidy mechanism, the constant level it quietly assumes, the evidence that the level was never constant, and then the corrections and limits that follow. Paragraphs 16 and 17 land it, calling the output a probability distribution rather than a year.
distractorNotes: Tree rings supply the correction, but the passage never claims anything about their value to other sciences.
The production chemistry is only the opening move, and most of the passage is about calibration.
Paragraph 12 presents the spike as a dating opportunity, and says the excess has largely drained away since.
Paragraph 12 treats the bomb curve as a gift for recent material, so the passage argues nearly the reverse.

questions.stem: The author pairs the weapons testing spike with fossil fuel dilution mainly in order to show that
choices: people have pushed the level both ways, with opposite effects on dating
burning fossil fuels released the neutrons that the weapons tests had produced
human activity has made modern samples impossible to date
the sun influences production more than any human activity does
the calibration curve has to be rebuilt from fresh tree rings every few decades

proof.quote: A second human signal runs the opposite way.
That steep decline is a gift.
could carry the radiocarbon signature of something several hundred years old
can often be placed within a year or two

questions.why: Paragraphs 12 and 13 are deliberately mirrored. The tests raised the level and opened a way to date recent tissue to within a year or two, and fossil carbon lowers it and may take that ability away.
distractorNotes: The tests released the neutrons themselves, while fossil fuels release carbon that carries no radiocarbon at all.
Paragraph 12 makes recent material easier to date rather than impossible, so this overstates the case.
Paragraph 12 opens by saying human activity moved the level far more violently than the sun ever did.
Rebuilding the curve on a schedule is never mentioned anywhere in the passage.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the way the passage is organized
choices: a chronological history of the people who developed the technique
a mechanism, then the assumption behind it, then the corrections its failure forces
a list of laboratory procedures arranged from the least to the most expensive
a comparison of radiocarbon dating with two competing dating methods
a problem stated at the very outset and a proposed solution that the author finally rejects

proof.quote: The mechanism is almost too tidy.
the founding assumption was the simplest one available
The correction came from trees.
the flaw that made all of this necessary

questions.why: Paragraphs 1 through 5 lay out a clean mechanism, paragraph 6 names the assumption it rests on and calls it wrong, and everything after that is correction and limitation. The last two paragraphs say what survives: a range with a probability attached.
distractorNotes: Dates appear, but no researcher is named and the material is not arranged as a history.
Pretreatment steps appear in paragraph 14, but cost is never discussed anywhere.
Uranium and thorium dating of corals appears once as a support for the curve, never as a rival.
The corrections are endorsed rather than rejected, and paragraph 17 calls the whole difficulty worth having.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the founding assumption that the atmospheric level never changed is best described as
choices: convinced that it still holds well enough for most practical laboratory work
puzzled that anyone would ever have proposed it
accepting of it as a sensible start that evidence later overturned
scornful of the carelessness it represented
indifferent, since it has no bearing on how dates are produced now

proof.quote: That is a sensible first approximation, and it is wrong.

questions.why: Paragraph 6 gives both halves in one breath. It calls the assumption a sensible first approximation and then says flatly that it is wrong, which is respect for the reasoning together with a clear verdict on it.
distractorNotes: The same paragraph says the assumption is wrong, and the rest of the passage corrects for it.
Calling something a sensible first approximation is the opposite of finding it baffling.
The word sensible rules out scorn, and the passage treats the assumption as reasonable for its moment.
The failure of that assumption drives the entire calibration enterprise, so it could hardly matter more.

questions.stem: In paragraph 16, the author's attitude toward the figure a laboratory reports is best described as
choices: confident in the measurement and wary of how it gets read
impressed by how precisely a calendar answer can now be fixed
irritated with laboratories for publishing an uncertainty at all
doubtful that radiocarbon measurements carry real information
resigned to the method being replaced by something better

proof.quote: it is tempting to read it as the calendar answer's error bar
It is not.
what emerges is lumpy

questions.why: Paragraph 16 never questions the measurement. What it questions is the instinct to read the plus or minus as a calendar error bar, and it answers that instinct with three blunt words.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 16 argues the reverse, since better counting precision buys almost nothing on a plateau.
The uncertainty is welcomed as honest reporting, and paragraph 17 treats the honest date as a probability distribution.
The passage treats the measurement as sound, and its caution is about interpretation rather than content.
No replacement is proposed anywhere, and paragraph 17 closes by calling the difficulty worth having.

questions.stem: The passage supports all of the following statements EXCEPT:
choices: The calibration curve reaches further back in time than the tree ring record does on its own
A milligram of material can be enough for a determination today
Carbon fourteen production rises and falls with the activity of the sun
Halving a laboratory's counting error always halves the width of the calendar range
An organism that feeds from the sea can seem centuries old on the day it dies

proof.quote: an active sun suppresses production and a quiet sun raises it
appear roughly four hundred years dead at the moment they actually die
Trees run out before the method does.
so a milligram is enough
halving the counting error barely narrows the calendar range

questions.why: Paragraph 16 says the intuition that a better measurement always buys a better date fails outright on a plateau, where halving the counting error barely narrows the calendar range. The other four statements are stated in paragraphs 6, 11, 10 and 15.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 8 gives the trees about twelve thousand years, and paragraph 10 carries the curve out to about fifty five thousand.
Paragraph 15 credits accelerator mass spectrometry with bringing the sample down to a milligram.
Paragraph 6 says an active sun suppresses production and a quiet sun raises it, so this one is supported.
Paragraph 11 puts marine organisms at roughly four hundred years dead at the moment they actually die.

questions.stem: A reader looking for how radiocarbon has been used to estimate a person's year of birth should turn to
choices: paragraph 12
paragraph 14
paragraph 3
paragraph 7
paragraph 16

proof.quote: has been used to estimate a person's year of birth

questions.why: Paragraph 12 closes with it. Because each year on the declining bomb curve carries its own value, tooth enamel laid down in childhood and never rebuilt can be matched to a year of birth.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 14 is about contamination, pretreatment and choosing a short lived sample.
Paragraph 3 covers how living tissue takes carbon fourteen in, not how recent tissue is dated.
Paragraph 7 is about Egyptian objects coming back too young, which is where the calibration problem first surfaced.
Paragraph 16 explains what a reported measurement means, not what has been dated with it.

questions.stem: A timber from a barn whose construction is documented in the year 1700 comes back about three centuries older than the barn. The passage's reasoning most directly supports which explanation?
choices: Rootlets and groundwater delivered recent carbon into the timber over the centuries
The heartwood grew long before felling, or the timber was reused from an older building
The laboratory counted decays in the sample instead of counting its atoms directly
The laboratory calculated the age from the newer half-life rather than the original value
The timber's carbon was drawn from deep ocean water long out of contact with the atmosphere

proof.quote: the heartwood of a beam grew centuries before the tree was felled, and beams were often salvaged and reused

questions.why: Paragraph 14 gives the rule: the heartwood of a beam grew centuries before the tree was felled, and beams were often salvaged and reused, so a timber can easily be older than the building it holds up. That is exactly why the passage prefers a seed, which lives one season.
distractorNotes: Rootlets and groundwater deliver recent carbon, and paragraph 14 shows recent carbon pulling a reported age toward the present, not away from it.
Paragraph 15 says the two instruments differ in how much sample they need, not in the age they report.
Paragraph 4 says laboratories still report ages from the original value, so no switch of half-life is in play.
Paragraph 11 reserves the marine offset for organisms that build tissue from sea water, and paragraph 3 has plants taking their carbon from the air.
